slide_001.text: Welcome to Module 2, Constructions and Materials. In this module, we will look at the main materials used in construction and industrial projects, their important properties, and the factors that influence material selection. We will also discuss how these materials behave in different environments and why their characteristics are important from an inspection and corrosion-protection point of view. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. The key points shown are MODULE 2 Constructions and Materials. slide_002.text: Let us begin with an overview of material selection. The materials covered in this module include iron and its alloys, low-alloy constructional steel, weathering steel, stainless steel, aluminium and its alloys, copper and its alloys, zinc, titanium, and concrete. These materials do not behave in the same way. Their strength, corrosion behaviour, weight, fabrication characteristics, and service limitations are different. Therefore, the correct material must be selected according to the intended service and environmental conditions. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_003.text: When selecting a construction material, several factors need to be considered. The material must have sufficient strength to carry the required load and enough flexibility to handle vibration or movement. Weight is important for transportation, lifting, handling, and support. We also consider whether the material can be formed into the required shape, its durability in the expected environment, and the amount of maintenance it may require. Initial material cost is important, but life-cycle cost gives a broader picture because it considers purchase, operation, inspection, maintenance, repair, and replacement over the service life. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. The key points shown are SELECTING CONSTRUCTION MATERIAL A number of factors may come into consideration when deciding on which material one should use to construct an object, such as: Its strength (to carry weight) Its flexibility (to handle vibration / movements) Its weight (to move / handle the object) Its ability to be formed into the required shape Its durability (against environmental conditions) Its need for maintenance work The cost of the material Life Cycle Cost (a combination of many of the above factors) 03. slide_004.text: Pure iron is generally too soft for construction use. It has relatively low strength and can bend or deform when subjected to heavy loads. When a controlled amount of carbon is added to iron, the material becomes steel. Other alloying elements can also be added to modify its performance. The amount of carbon, the type of alloying elements, heat treatment, and manufacturing process determine the properties of each steel grade. In this way, steel can be designed to provide properties such as strength, hardness, ductility, toughness, corrosion resistance, and heat resistance. slide_005.text: Carbon steel is mainly an alloy of iron and carbon. The carbon content can be up to about two percent, and small amounts of elements such as manganese, silicon, sulfur, and phosphorus may also be present. Carbon plays an important role in the properties of the steel. Increasing carbon generally increases strength and hardness. However, if the carbon content becomes too high, ductility and toughness reduce and the steel can become hard and brittle. Therefore, carbon content must be controlled according to the required application and performance. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_006.text: Carbon steel can be grouped according to its carbon content. Low carbon steel contains approximately zero to 0.30 percent carbon and includes products such as mild steel sheets and structural sections. Medium carbon steel contains about 0.31 to 0.60 percent carbon. It is stronger, but more difficult to form, weld, and cut, and may be used for railway axles and automotive shafts. High carbon steel contains about 0.61 to 1.0 percent carbon and is difficult to cut, bend, and weld. Ultra-high carbon steel ranges from about 1.0 to 2.0 percent and can be used for high-hardness tools and blades. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_007.text: Alloy steel is produced by combining iron and carbon with selected alloying elements. Common alloying elements include chromium, nickel, molybdenum, manganese, vanadium, copper, and silicon. These elements are added to give the steel specific properties and improve its performance for the intended application. For example, alloying can improve strength, toughness, hardenability, wear resistance, corrosion resistance, or high-temperature performance. In this module, low-alloy steel includes weathering steel, while high-alloy steels include stainless steel and duplex stainless steel. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_008.text: Weathering steel is a type of low-alloy steel designed for improved resistance to atmospheric corrosion. When exposed to suitable weather conditions over time, it develops a rust-coloured protective oxide layer called a patina. This layer slows further atmospheric corrosion and can allow the steel to be used without painting in suitable atmospheric environments. However, weathering steel is not suitable for all conditions. It should be carefully considered for immersion, persistent dampness, marine or coastal chloride exposure, and other environments where the protective patina cannot develop properly. It is also used in applications such as some shipping-container steels. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_009.text: Weathering steel has several advantages. In suitable atmospheric exposure, the protective patina can reduce or eliminate the need for painting, while ordinary carbon steel normally requires protective coating. The patina also gives the material a characteristic decorative appearance and improves resistance to atmospheric corrosion. However, there are limitations. The initial rust-like appearance may be considered unattractive before the stable patina develops. Patina formation depends strongly on climate and environmental conditions. Aggressive environments may still require protective coating, and welding and fabrication require appropriate procedures and compatible consumables. slide_010.text: Stainless steel is a high-alloy steel containing sufficient chromium to form a protective passive film. The slide describes a minimum chromium content of 10.5 percent by weight and less than 1.2 percent carbon, with other alloying elements such as nickel, molybdenum, titanium, niobium, and manganese depending on the grade. Chromium forms a thin chromium-oxide passive layer on the surface. Nickel and molybdenum may be added to improve specific properties, including corrosion resistance. Stainless steel is corrosion resistant, but it is not corrosion proof. If passivity breaks down, localized corrosion such as pitting, crevice corrosion, or stress-corrosion cracking can occur, particularly in chloride environments. slide_011.text: Stainless steel provides a combination of useful properties. Important advantages include high corrosion resistance, good strength, good heat resistance, good toughness, and good chemical resistance. It can provide a long service life and relatively low maintenance when the correct grade is selected for the service environment. Stainless steel also has a clean and attractive appearance and can be welded and fabricated using suitable procedures. These advantages explain why stainless steel is widely used where corrosion resistance, hygiene, appearance, durability, and long-term performance are important. slide_012.text: Stainless steel also has disadvantages that must be considered during material selection. Its initial cost is generally higher than conventional carbon steel. Some grades require greater control during welding and fabrication, including suitable procedures, skilled personnel, clean tools, and control of contamination. Chloride and salt environments can create risks such as pitting, crevice corrosion, and stress-corrosion cracking when an unsuitable grade is selected. Localized corrosion may penetrate deeply with limited visible warning. For these reasons, stainless steel is not automatically the best choice for every construction application. Grade, environment, fabrication, maintenance, and life-cycle cost must all be considered. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_013.text: Duplex stainless steel is a type of high-alloy stainless steel. According to the slide, it contains more than 18 percent chromium and has a microstructure containing both austenitic and ferritic phases. This combination provides higher strength than conventional austenitic stainless steels such as 304 and 316. Duplex stainless steel is widely used in demanding industries including oil and gas, petrochemical, marine, chemical, and offshore applications. Its selection is normally linked to the need for strength and corrosion resistance in challenging service conditions. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. slide_014.text: Duplex stainless steel offers high toughness, high corrosion resistance, and high chemical resistance. In suitable atmospheric conditions, painting may not be required. However, the material also has important limitations. Its cost is higher than carbon steel, fabrication can be more difficult, and welding and inspection require skilled personnel and appropriate procedures. The slide also notes that coating may still be required in very aggressive C5 or CX environments. Therefore, duplex stainless steel should be selected based on the actual service environment and project requirements rather than assuming that its corrosion resistance removes every need for protection. slide_015.text: Ductile cast iron is one type of cast iron and the slide identifies a carbon content of about three percent. Compared with grey cast iron, ductile cast iron provides better ductility and toughness. It can tolerate bending, twisting, or deformation to a greater extent without fracturing and is generally stronger and tougher than grey cast iron. These properties make it useful for components such as pipes, valves, gears, pumps, and pressure parts. The key point is that its composition and structure provide a useful combination of castability, strength, and ductility for engineering applications. slide_016.text: Steel rolling is a metal-forming process in which steel passes between rotating rolls. The purpose is to reduce thickness, change the cross-sectional shape, or produce the required dimensions. Rolling can also influence the mechanical properties of the steel. The two main rolling methods shown here are hot rolling and cold rolling. The important difference is the temperature at which the material is processed, and this affects the surface condition, achievable thickness, dimensions, and the presence or absence of mill scale. slide_017.text: Let us compare hot-rolled and cold-rolled steel. Hot-rolled steel is rolled at high temperature and mill scale is normally present on the surface. The slide also notes the use of smaller rollers and that a wide range of thicknesses can be achieved. Cold-rolled steel is rolled at room temperature and does not form the same mill scale associated with hot rolling. It is used for thinner products, with the slide indicating thicknesses usually below four millimetres. An important corrosion point is that mill scale is cathodic to the base steel, so its presence and condition are important during surface preparation and coating work. The slide highlights limitations for structural use in situations where high-temperature resistance is required and notes that aluminium can experience corrosion problems in marine environments. The slide gives a typical curing period of approximately thirty days at room temperature and notes that the form may be removed after about two days. Moisture is required during curing. If the concrete is allowed to dry too early, the curing reaction can be affected. After curing, additional drying is required before coating so that excess moisture does not interfere with coating adhesion and performance. On this slide, we will develop the topic step by step. Concrete cover separates the reinforcement from the external environment and helps protect the steel from moisture and contaminants. slide_031.text: Steel reinforcement bars, or rebars, are used in concrete to resist tensile, shear, and bending stresses because concrete itself is relatively weak in tension. Rebars are commonly left uncoated and depend on the concrete environment for protection. The slide explains that when concrete carbonation reduces the alkalinity, the protection of the steel can be lost. If corrosion then develops, the corrosion products occupy a larger volume than the original steel. This expansion can create internal pressure, cracking, delamination, and spalling of the surrounding concrete. Protecting the reinforcement is therefore essential for long-term structural durability. slide_032.text: This slide illustrates the corrosion mechanism of reinforcement inside concrete. Initially, the alkaline concrete environment helps protect the embedded steel. As carbonation progresses from the exposed surface, the pH can fall and the protective condition around the reinforcement can be reduced. When moisture and oxygen are available, corrosion can start. The rust products expand around the bar, creating pressure within the concrete. Over time, this can lead to cracking and spalling. The visual is a reminder that deterioration may begin.

slide_033.text: Coated and uncoated reinforcement provide different levels of protection. Coated rebar adds a protective barrier between the steel and moisture or corrosive substances. This can reduce corrosion, rust staining, cracking, and spalling and may extend the service life of reinforced concrete. Uncoated rebar has no additional coating barrier and therefore relies more directly on the protection provided by the surrounding concrete. If corrosion develops, expansion of the corrosion products can damage the concrete. The appropriate choice depends on the exposure environment and project durability requirements. These checks should be completed before coating application so that the coating is applied to a sound, clean, dry, and properly prepared concrete surface. slide_037.text: Laitance is a weak and friable layer that can appear on the surface of concrete after curing. The slide explains that it can occur when too much water is present and that new concrete commonly has some degree of laitance. Its thickness can range from fine dust to several millimetres. If it is not removed, the paint may adhere to the weak laitance rather than to sound concrete, which can lead to adhesion failure. Suitable removal methods include shot blasting, power-tool preparation, scrabbling, grinding, abrading, and low-pressure blasting.
